title: A light-travel-time clock can stall the ASASSN-14ko period only for a black hole above about 1e8 solar masses seen edge-on, and it predicts no decrease after 2024, against the 2026 flare
abstract: Question: the period of the repeating nuclear transient ASASSN-14ko decreased fast before 2020, stayed constant in 2020-2024 (X-ray clock) and became shorter again after 2024. Wu et al. (2024) proposed that the period change is a light-travel-time (Roemer) effect: the star orbits an intermediate-mass black hole that orbits the central supermassive black hole (SMBH). A Roemer clock stops a period change naturally. Approach: we repeated their calculation, then fitted a constant intrinsic period plus the exact Keplerian Roemer delay to 61 flare markers of 2014-2026 (X-ray suppression, UV, optical, TESS and SPHEREx times from signed SCI publications), with the amplitude bounded by a/c for each SMBH mass. We also trained all clocks on 2014-2021 data and scored their forecasts of 2022-2026 with nested sampling. Results: the published estimate dP/dt = Delta d/(cP) equals v_r/c, a Doppler factor, not the period derivative P a_r/c; their model gives at most |Pdot| = 0.0015 over 22 cycles and fits the flare times worse than a constant Pdot by 2 Delta lnL = 82. A correct Roemer clock is worse than a constant Pdot for SMBH masses up to the host value (10^7.86 Msun), equal at 10^7.95 and better by Delta AIC = 8-21 above 10^8.05, always with an edge-on outer orbit. With the host mass as prior, the posterior needs log10 M_BH = 8.19-8.80 (95%) and the Bayes factor is about e^2. Bounded Roemer clocks predict no period decrease after 2024 and put the 2026 TESS flare 5-8 d later than observed (2.6-2.7 sigma). Trained on 2014-2021 data, Roemer clocks forecast the stall (log predictive density -87 to -89, against -149 for a constant Pdot and -245 for a cubic), but random period kicks do as well (-84). These results hold without the 2022 optical peaks and with another X-ray marker. Limitations: the host mass is uncertain by a factor of about 2.5, and a mass above 10^8.2 Msun keeps the Roemer clock viable; marker classes have constant offsets; post-2024 evidence rests on four cycles; we did not measure line velocities, which must change by about 6,000 km/s between 2014 and 2020 in this model. Chandra data of 2026 June-July (public from December 2026) and flare-line velocities can test it.

display.caption: All 61 ASASSN-14ko flare markers (2014-2026) relative to a linear 108.437-d clock, with five clock fits, and the period change per cycle of each fit. Roemer (light-travel-time) clocks with a bounded black-hole mass give a fast decrease near 2017-2019, a stall and no decrease after 2024; the 2026 TESS flare is earlier than they predict.

Best Roemer clock for each upper bound on the SMBH mass, relative to a constant period derivative. The Roemer clock is better only for masses above about 1e8 solar masses, at the upper end of the host estimate (orange). Cross: the published model M05 of Wu et al. (2024).

Clocks trained on 2014-2021 data only and their forecasts of the 20 markers of 2022-2026. Constant-Pdot and cubic clocks fail; Roemer clocks and random period kicks forecast the stall about equally well.
